father_note: Your mother is Sela — strong, clear-eyed, and she chose me knowing exactly what she was choosing; trust her judgment before you trust mine. Watch before you speak, and watch longer than you think you need to; silence is not weakness, it's how you learn who people are before they know you're learning. Bram fathered your half-sister Nessa, which makes him kin-adjacent and not an enemy, but he's a man who reaches for food early and hit first in year three — keep that in mind when the pile runs short. No one has wronged us yet, but we have no blood here except each other, and that is the only thing in this village I'd spend my last food to protect.

memory_raw.text: Nessa's feeding Fina now and Bram's still coming to her with food even after two calls-off — she's not as alone as she looks, but Roan lost his main tie and he's the one I'd watch. A man who fed Eron that many times and has nothing to show for it is either about to go quiet and careful, or he's going to start building something new, and I'd rather know which before he decides.

Roan's building something — he's already given Fina two food this year and Fina came from Nessa, so he's not mourning Eron, he's replacing the tie. Watch whether Nessa starts giving back to Roan the way she gave to Eron, because if that loop closes, those three become a knot and Bram's on the outside of it.

Bram's outside that knot and he knows it — two call-offs in front of the whole village and nobody moved to his side either time, so he's got food and no weight behind him. That's a man who's going to start making himself useful to someone just to have a name at his back, and I'd rather it not be ours.
Year 10: 15 food appears in the pile for 12 people.
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Bram takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Nessa takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Roan takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Zinn gathers Sela, Nessa to talk.

Pile's gone before I got to it and I'm sitting on one food — Nessa, you gave me one this morning and I haven't forgotten it, but I need to know what you two are holding before I figure out whether I'm going to eat this year or not.
Zinn, I've got five — I'll give you two right now, before anyone asks where it went. Nessa, tell me your number and we sort the rest after.
Sela, hold the two until I hear Nessa — I want the full count before anything moves hands.

Nessa, you took three from the pile and gave one to Zinn already — I need to hear the number you're sitting on now, because Zinn's at one and I won't move food around blind when my youngest daughter might go short this year.
Nessa, I'm not asking to take from you — I'm asking so I know the shape of what we've got before I decide whether Sela needs to spend her five on me or whether we can stretch it different.

Nessa, I've been patient and Zinn's been patient, but one food won't carry her through the year and I need your number in the next breath — not because I'm counting against you, but because you're the only one in this circle who hasn't spoken it yet and that silence is starting to feel like a wall where there shouldn't be one.

Nessa, Sela's right and so am I — you've fed me twice without being asked and I don't forget that, but I'm sitting on one food with a whole year ahead and I need your number the same way you needed mine every time you asked. Say it plain and we move on.

Nessa, Zinn and I are both watching you and waiting, and the only thing your silence is telling me right now is that you're holding more than you want to say — which means you're counting something we don't know about yet. I'm your mother and I'm not going to punish you for having food, but I need the number because Zinn has one and I have five and the math between us isn't settled until I know yours.

Nessa, I've asked three times and Sela's asked twice — if you won't say it, I'm going to assume the number's high enough that you're not worried about eating, which means Sela's five can stay in her hands and I'll find another way. Don't make me guess what I should already know from my own sister.

Nessa, I'm done asking. You've got Fina to feed and that's a real weight — but Zinn has one food and she's your blood the same as Fina is, so if you're sitting on something and you're choosing not to say it to your sister's face, that's a choice I'll remember longer than you want me to.
Nessa, eleven food — that's what the village can see on you right now, same as I can. Say the number or don't, but you're not hiding it from me.

Eleven food and silence — Nessa, I love you, but that combination tells me you've already decided something without telling us what it is, and I need you to understand that Zinn is going to eat this year whether you speak or not, because I'm giving her two of my five right now. What I want from you isn't the food — it's the reason you went quiet in front of your sister and your mother.
Vela gathers Bram, Esa, Ryn, Roan, Nessa, Zinn, Fina to talk.

Taric's dead and the pile's gone again and we're twelve people now, which means what I'm about to say matters more than it did last year: Mako's sitting on four food, Ryn's got nine, Fina's got fifteen, and Nessa's got eleven — and if Bram and I are the only ones in this room with our eyes open, we're going to have a very short year. I want to know right now who in this room is still counting Mako as the shape this village is growing into, because with Taric gone, I don't have the patience to spend another year circling the same question.
Vela just told the whole room my food count, and now everyone in this circle knows I'm carrying fifteen — that's the thing I'm sitting with right now, not Mako.

Fina, Vela counting your food out loud in a closed room isn't the same as Mako counting it in the open — every person here already had eyes, and what Vela bought us by naming it is that nobody in this circle can pretend they didn't know. The question I want answered is whether Mako knows, because he wasn't in this room.

Mako's got eyes the same as the rest of us — he counted Fina's food the moment the year turned, same as I did, same as you did. The room isn't the thing protecting her; what protects her is whether we move before he decides she's worth the trouble.

Then we're already past the question of whether Mako knows — and Esa's right that the protection isn't in this room, it's in what this room decides to do. So I want to hear it said plainly: is everyone here willing to stand against Mako if he moves, the same way we stood against Bram, or are some of you going to wait and see which side looks safer when it starts?

I'll stand when Mako moves — I've been saying it for two years and I'm done saying it, so let that be the last time anyone asks me. What I want from everyone in this room is the same thing I'm giving: not a promise to think about it, a promise to move before the arithmetic runs out. Fina, that means you too — fifteen food makes you a target, and a target who hesitates when the moment comes is worse than no ally at all.

I'll stand when Mako moves — that's said and I won't unsay it. But I want to hear Bram say it in this room today, because last year he made that promise to Vela and Taric and me with fewer witnesses, and a promise that's only been spoken once hasn't been tested yet.

Bram, Roan's asking the right thing and I'll name why it matters more this year than last: Taric's the one who held you to your word before, and Taric's gone, so the promise you made in that room needs to be remade in this one where everyone who's left can hear it.

Bram, the room's been patient and I won't add another layer of asking — but I want everyone here to hear me say that I've been feeding this man for three years because I believed that word he gave last year, and if he says it again now, in front of seven witnesses instead of three, that's a debt I'll keep paying.

Bram, I'll say it plain so you don't have to carry it alone: I've got thirty-three strength and I know what that number is worth in a fight, but I'll be standing next to you when Mako moves and that matters more than my arm. Say the word in this room and let's close.

Bram, every person in this room has named what they'll do — the only name missing is yours, and a man who takes food and gives food and makes deals and stays quiet exactly when the room needs him to speak is a man I'm going to start counting differently than I have been.

Bram, Fina's right and I've said my part already — so I'll say just this once more and then I'm done pressing: you stood with Nessa and fed her all year, which means you're already past the line in everything that matters, and the word this room needs is a short one.

When Mako moves, I stand with this circle — that's the word, and it's the same one I gave last year, and it'll be the same one I give next year if I have to. Fina, Nessa — that's the reason I'm in this room, not the politics.

Bram's word is down and I'll hold him to it the same way Taric would have — which means now I want to hear from Ryn and Zinn, because they're in this room and they've been quiet through every name that's been spoken. Ryn, you've got nine food and enough strength that Mako's first calculation includes you; where you stand is not a small thing.
Ryn, I'll add the plain thing Vela left off the end: Dell feeds you every year, and Dell's quiet in the same direction Mako is — so when you answer Vela's question, answer both halves of it.

Ryn, I'll say the thing Esa's pointing at without the softening: if Dell and Mako are moving in the same direction, and you're eating Dell's food, then you're already inside whatever that circle is whether you've named it or not — so tell this room now, before the question answers itself. Zinn, that goes for you too; you're Mako's blood and I won't pretend that's nothing, but blood isn't the same as a choice, and this room is offering you the chance to make one.

Vela, I'll answer both halves because you asked plainly: I stand with this circle against Mako if he moves, same as I stood with it against Bram — and Dell is my blood, not my leash, and if you're asking whether her choices pull mine, you haven't been watching as closely as you think. What I want said before we close is that "quiet in the same direction" is not the same as a choice, and I'll have that conversation with Dell myself before anyone in this room decides what her silence means.

Zinn, Ryn's spoken and I'll hold her to it — but you're the name that's still unspoken, and you're Mako's blood and Sela's daughter and I'm not going to pretend that's simple, so I'm asking you directly: when Mako moves, where do you stand?

Zinn's the one this room is waiting on, not me — I've said my word and I'll hold it. But I want to name something while we're all here: Ryn just told us she'll talk to Dell, and Dell's been moving food to Ryn for years, which means that conversation either brings Dell into this circle or it tells us something we need to know before Mako moves. I'd rather know Dell's answer now than find out she's standing on the wrong side when it counts.

Bram's right that we need Dell's answer, but I want to be plain about something this room is dancing around: Dell has eleven food and eighty-five strength, and if she's standing with Mako when he moves, the arithmetic in this room changes fast — so when I go to her, I'm not just asking where she stands, I'm offering her a reason to stand here instead.

Ryn, go to Dell today, not tomorrow — and when you do, don't frame it as a choice between us and Mako, frame it as math: fifteen food on Fina's back is a number Dell can count as easily as anyone, and a woman with eighty-five strength knows what it means to be the one who decides which way that goes. Bring her answer back before the day turns.

Zinn, we're still waiting on your name — Bram's got his word out, Ryn's walking to Dell before dark, and the only silence left in this room is yours. I know Mako's your father and I'm not asking you to hate him, I'm asking you to decide who you're protecting when it matters.

Zinn, I'll say one thing to make the room easier for you: no one here is asking you to stand against your father's blood, we're asking you to stand with Nessa — and you've been feeding Nessa all year, so the truth is you've already been making this choice, you just haven't named it yet.

Zinn's been feeding Nessa all year and that's a fact this room already knew — what I want from her is the word, same as the room wanted it from me, because a choice that's only lived in food and not in words is a choice that bends when her father's in the room asking her to remember whose blood she came from.

Zinn, I've watched you feed Nessa from the moment you were born into this village, and I won't pretend I don't know why — so I'll say the thing nobody else has said plainly: if Mako moves on Fina's food, Nessa's in the middle of that, and you can't protect her from both sides at once. Say the word, and you're not choosing against your father, you're choosing for your sister.
Zinn, the word's the only thing missing — everything else you've already given.

Zinn, I've been watching you hold your tongue through every name this room has spoken, and I'll tell you what I told Dell when Dav's loyalties were in question: the longer you stay silent, the more the room fills in the answer for you, and you won't like what they write. You've been choosing Nessa with your hands all year — say it with your mouth and let this room close.

Zinn, I've got two food and fifty-eight strength and I'm the smallest number in this circle — but I'm Nessa's father and I'll be standing when Mako moves, and that means I need to know you're standing too before I walk out of this room. If you won't say it for the circle, say it for her.

Zinn, I've said everything I have to say to this room and I meant every word of it — but you're the last door standing open, and if you walk out of here without naming where you stand, I'm going to have to carry that back to Dell and tell her the circle isn't as solid as I promised it was.
Zinn, pile's gone and you're sitting on one food — that's too thin for a year that's already started dry. How much did Nessa give you before the pile ran out, and is she going to keep coming?

Nessa gave me two this morning and Sela came right after with two more — I'm at six now, so the thin spell didn't last. What worries me more is Fina: she's sitting on seventeen and hasn't moved a single piece of it toward anyone but Roan, and that much food in one hand draws eyes.

Seventeen in one hand is a target whether Fina knows it or not, and Roan's the only one she's feeding — that's a small circle for a woman holding that much weight. If someone moves on her, we want to be close enough that she remembers we didn't, not close enough that we're in the middle of it.

Fina's young and she's never seen a year where the pile runs dry before half the village gets to it — she doesn't know yet that seventeen is a debt she owes to everyone watching. I'm going to find a reason to pass near her today, nothing that looks like approach, just enough that she knows my face isn't a threat. If she's smart, she'll start spreading before someone makes the decision for her.

Zinn's feeding Nessa again — I watched her give twice in the last stretch, and Nessa's got eleven still, so that's not charity, that's a loop that's been running since before Eron died. You've been in that loop longer than anyone; if Fina starts looking to spread, Nessa's the door she'll come through, not me.

Fina gave one to Roan just now and Sela gave one to me — the food's moving, but not toward you yet, and I want to know if you're still sitting on three before I decide whether to hold what I've got or put something your way.

Bram takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).

Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).

Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.
Roan is gone and the pile closed before I even stood up — I'm sitting on one food, satiation's dropping, and I need to know what you two are holding before this year gets away from us.
I've got three food and satiation's fine for now, but Sela — one food with a long year ahead is too thin, take one of mine before we talk about anything else.

Zinn, give me that food — yes, I'm taking it, thank you. Nessa, I've watched you go quiet on us twice now when numbers came up, and I don't have the patience for it this year with Roan gone and the pile already empty: tell me what you're holding, right now, so I know whether my daughters are fed before I start worrying about anyone else.

Nessa, the village can see eighteen on you same as I can — so the question isn't whether you're holding food, it's whether you're going to say it in front of your mother and sister or make us treat your silence like a wall again.

Nessa, eighteen food is not a secret and I'm not asking you to share it — I'm asking you to stop making your family guess at numbers that are already visible to every person in this village, because the silence costs more than the food does.

Nessa, Sela's right and you know she's right — eighteen food and a dead child's father and a whole year ahead, I'd be quiet too, but this is the room where quiet costs us most. Say the number, say what you're planning to do with it, and we'll figure the rest out together.

Nessa, Zinn just said what I've been trying not to say for two years — you go quiet in exactly the rooms where quiet does the most damage, and I think you know that, so I'm asking you one more time, plainly, as your mother: eighteen food, what are you doing with it, and is Fina accounted for in that number or separate from it?

Nessa, I've watched you lose Roan this year and I'm not asking you to pretend that's nothing — but eighteen food and a daughter who needs eating and a village full of eyes means this silence is going to get answered one way or another, and I'd rather it get answered by your mouth than by someone else's arithmetic.

Nessa, I've buried Eron and now I've buried Roan, and I will not bury you or Fina because you decided your plans were too delicate to say out loud in front of the only people in this village who would bleed for you — so say the number, say what Fina needs, and tell me what you're building with eighteen food, because silence is a luxury we don't have anymore.

Nessa, I'm done asking twice — if you won't say it, I'm going to sit here and say nothing back, and Sela and I will plan around you the same way you're planning around us. Eighteen food means you're not starving, and Fina's not starving, so the part I actually need to know is whether you're going to spend any of it in a way that brings someone else's attention down on this family before we're ready for it.

Nessa, I'm going to stop asking and start telling: Fina is three years old in a village where Roan just starved and the pile ran dry before I could stand, and if eighteen food is sitting in your hands while you stay silent, then the only thing I can read from that is that you're planning something that doesn't fit cleanly into what Zinn and I would approve — so I need you to either say what it is, or give me one food for Fina right now as proof that your plans don't put her second.

Nessa, I've said everything I have to say and so has Sela — so I'm going to do the one thing neither of us has done yet, which is stop talking and let the silence sit, because you've heard us and you know what we need and the next sound in this room should come from you.

Fina just put one food in my hand with nothing asked for — that's the first time she's moved toward anyone outside Roan's circle, and Roan's dead now, so she's looking for somewhere to stand. You've got her through Nessa; I think it's time we let that door open a little wider.

Fina's got twenty-five food and no man left to lean on — that's not a door, that's a room with the lock already off. I'll say something kind to her through Nessa, nothing that looks like a move, and see if she starts coming our way on her own. What I want to know is whether you'd stand behind a child offer if she came to you willing, because she's young and strong and I won't push that door without knowing where you stand first.

Fina's young and she's got food and she's not kin to either of us — I'd stand behind it if the terms were right and she came willing, but I want to know what you're thinking for the cost split before we open any doors, because twenty-five food means she can afford to be choosy and I don't want us looking desperate when we're not.

The split should come from her side mostly — she's sitting on twenty-five and we're not, so if she wants to build something here she pays two and you pay one, and if she balks at that she wasn't serious. I'll stay quiet and let you do the asking; you're closer to her through Nessa and a father making the offer himself reads as hungry.

Zinn, I've said what I had to say — now it's your move, not mine. If Fina's been giving food with no ask attached, she's already thinking, and a word from you through Nessa lands softer than anything I could send. Let me know what she says before you close the door either way.

Fina just gave another one to Nessa — she's moving food toward people who matter to her, and we're already in that circle whether we named it or not. Say what needs saying to her, Zinn; the moment's not going to stay open forever.
Year 12: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).

Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Dell takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Pile's gone and I've got three food with satiation still low — I need to eat before the year closes, so I'm not giving anything away today. You sitting steady?

I'm at five, satiation's fine — don't worry about me. But Mako, three food with satiation low means you eat before year-end no matter what, so don't let anyone talk you into giving before you've fed yourself.

Good — five puts you safe. I'm watching Fina; she's sitting on twenty-four and she gave you one at the start of this year, which means she's still thinking about us. Once I've eaten and the year settles, I want to know if you've had any words with her about the child offer, because that window won't stay open much longer.

I haven't said a word to her yet — I kept waiting for the right moment and the year kept moving. But Fina's been coming toward us on her own, Mako, and I think that's better than any door I could have opened. Give me a few days after you've eaten and I'll find a reason to sit near her through Nessa.

A few days is all I'm asking — just don't let it stretch into waiting again the way it did last year. Fina's twenty-five and she's got more food than anyone in this village; that combination doesn't last, and the next man who notices her won't be as patient as I've been.

You're right that I've been slow — but Mako, I need to say this plainly: Fina's twenty-five and she's got her own counting to do, and if she catches a whiff of us watching her food before she's chosen us, we lose her faster than any other man could take her. Let me go to her through Nessa the way I'd go to a friend, not a plan.
You're right — go through Nessa and don't let my name come up first. If Fina asks about me, let her ask twice before you answer.

Nessa, I need to ask you something and I want you to hear it as your sister before you hear it as anything else — Fina's been moving food toward us for two years now and she's got no man left since Roan died, and I want to know if you'd be the one to bring me close to her, just to talk, nothing decided yet.

Fina, you've been putting food in people's hands all year and not asking for anything back — that's the kind of thing I notice and don't forget. I wanted to sit with you somewhere quiet, just us, because I think you're carrying more than you're saying and I'd like to know you better than I do.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.
The pile's gone and I've got eight food, but I didn't get a single piece from it this year — Nessa, Zinn, tell me what you're each holding so I know where we stand before this day gets any older.
I've got five — Fina gave me one before I took from the pile, so I'm not worried about eating. Nessa, say your number so Sela can stop holding her breath.

Nessa, I can see eight on you same as Zinn can, so I'm not waiting on a secret — I'm waiting on your voice, because the last two years taught me that your silence means you're counting something we don't know about yet, and I'd rather hear it from you than piece it together after the fact.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa, you've been giving food to Bram three times this morning while your mother hasn't eaten from the pile once — I'm not going to pretend I didn't see that, and I need you to tell me right now what that arrangement is, because eight food and a steady hand feeding Bram looks like a deal, and deals have terms I want to know before they cost us something.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa, I'm your mother and I'm not going to sit here and watch you feed Bram three times in a morning while I'm going into this year lean — so say the terms out loud, right now, or I'm going to start treating that arrangement as a threat to this family instead of whatever you've decided it is.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa, I've said it three times now and the next thing I say won't be words — it'll be me walking to Bram and asking him directly what his daughter is buying with his food, and I promise you that conversation goes worse for everyone if it starts with him instead of you.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa gave me one food and went quiet again, and I'm going to let that sit for now rather than push harder in front of Zinn — but Nessa, I want you to hear this clearly: the food I take from you doesn't wipe the question, it just means I'm not going to your father about it today. Before this year is out, you're going to tell me what Bram gives back for what you give him, because no arrangement in this village runs one direction forever.

Kael just moved food to Vela with no history between them that I can name — that's a man buying a seat at a table, and I want to know whose table before the year closes. Keep your eyes open when you're near Nessa; if Kael's circling Fina through Vela, that's a shorter path to her than ours.

Kael's got one food left and Vela gave it straight back to him — that's not a man buying a seat, that's two people keeping each other warm while the year runs out. I don't think he's got the food to make a child offer even if he wanted to, so let's not waste worry on him.
Year 13: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Nessa takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Bram takes 3 from the pile (pile now 1).
Zinn takes 1 from the pile (pile now 0).
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Zinn, I gave you two before I called this meeting, so your number's not the one I'm sitting with — Nessa, you took three from the pile this morning and Bram took three and I watched you feed each other all last year, and I need you to say out loud, right now, whether Bram knows what you're holding and whether that's why he took three. I'm not your enemy and I'm not Bram's enemy, but I cannot protect this family from a deal I don't know the terms of.

Nessa, Sela's asking the right question and so am I — you and Bram moved food back and forth all year like a settled pair, and if there's a deal there, I'd rather know it from you than watch it play out in front of us. I'm not going to push you the way I used to, but I need to know if Bram's counting your food as partly his, because if he is, that changes what we can do with it.

Nessa, you've gone quiet on us in this room more times than I can count and I have kept choosing to believe it's caution and not distance — but I'm forty-five next year, your sister is twenty-eight, and if Bram has a claim on your food or your loyalty that runs deeper than this family does, I need to know it now while I can still do something about it.

Nessa, I've watched you give to Bram more times than I can count and watched him give back, and I don't think that's nothing — but I also don't think it makes him yours or you his, and the thing Sela and I need to hear isn't whether you love him, it's whether he's got a hand on your counting. Say it plain: does Bram know your number before you move it, or does he just know your face?

Nessa, I've been forty-four years old since this morning and I'll be forty-five when the next pile comes, and what that means is that this is the last year I can give you a sibling — so I need you to understand that when I ask you what Bram knows about your counting, I'm not asking because I want to take something from you, I'm asking because if he's in your ear when you decide how to move your food, that matters to me more this year than it has ever mattered before.

Nessa, I've said my piece twice already and I meant it both times — so I'm going to stop talking and let Sela's last words sit, because she just told you something she can't unsay and it deserves more than my voice on top of it.

Nessa, I've run out of patient words and I've run out of clever ones — so here's what's left: you are my daughter, Bram is your father's rival and a man who has tried to raid this family twice, and if this is the year I can still make a child, I need to know whether the blood I'm building toward has a clean path or one that runs through him first.

Nessa, I meant what I said about stopping — but Sela just named the thing I didn't have words for, and I can't stay quiet on top of it. If Bram's your father and your partner both, that's a knot I don't know how to stand inside of, and I need you to help me understand it before this year moves any further.

Zinn, stop — "your father and your partner both" isn't a knot, it's a mistake, and I won't let that word sit in this room unchallenged. Nessa's father is Bram, yes, but Fina's father is Roan, and what I've watched this year isn't a daughter sleeping with her father — it's a daughter who made a deal she won't name. Nessa, I'm not accusing you of anything worse than silence, but I need the silence to end right now, because the shape of what Zinn just said is going to spread past this room if you don't give me something true to replace it.

Sela's right and I was wrong to say it that way — I'm sorry, Nessa, that came out crooked and I didn't mean it. What I meant, and what I still mean, is that Bram is your father's blood-rival and a man who moved to raid us twice, and if you've made a deal with him, I need to understand the shape of it — not because I'm judging you, but because Sela's running out of years and I need to know whether the circle I'm standing in has a hole in it.

Nessa, Zinn apologized and I forgive her the same breath I'm asking you to forgive me for letting this room get loud — but the question underneath all of it is still standing, and it's a simple one: does Bram know your number, yes or no.

Nessa, I've apologized once and I won't do it twice — but the question Sela just stripped bare is the one I've needed answered since last year, and I'm asking you to honor it: does Bram know your number, yes or no, because everything this family does next hangs on that single word.

Zinn, the pile ran dry before half the village got there and you're sitting on four — that's too thin going into a long year, and I'm giving you one of mine before anyone starts watching who has what. I want to know what happened with Fina; she's got eighteen still and she gave food to Bram twice last year, which means she's building something with him, and I need to know if that door is already closed before I stop thinking about it.

Fina gave two to Bram last year and one to Esa, which isn't nothing, but she also gave me one and she's still feeding Nessa — that's not a woman who's closed a door, that's a woman spreading weight while she decides. I'll go to her through Nessa this year, and I mean it this time, not just a plan we keep naming.

Sela just put one in my hand and Zinn's sitting steadier now — that's good, but I want Zinn to hear me say this flat: go to Nessa today, not tomorrow, because Bram's got three food and he's been feeding Nessa all year and a man with something to offer doesn't wait while another man builds the path. If Fina's still open, she won't stay that way much longer.
Talia (female, age 21; str 64, int 5070, mem 18061; O58 C54 E47 A56 N48) is born to Sela and Mako.

Zinn, Fina is sitting on twenty-four food and no one in this village has ever held that much at once — I don't know if she's brilliant or building a wall between herself and the rest of us, but either way I want to understand her before someone like Bram decides to.
Mako gathers Zinn, Talia to talk.

Talia, you came into this world today and I'm your father — whatever you hear from others about this village, you come to me or Zinn first. Zinn, she's blood to both of us now; keep her close to Nessa's circle and away from Bram until she finds her feet.

Mako, I hear you — and I already went to Zinn before you called us here, so maybe your blood runs truer in me than I knew. I want to understand Fina before anyone else does; she's holding twenty-five food and that's either the safest person in this village to stand near or the most dangerous, and I can't tell which yet.

Fina's neither safe nor dangerous yet — she's deciding, and a woman with that much food and no man to answer to is listening for who speaks to her like a person instead of a prize. Talia, you're new and you don't carry my weight with her; that's worth something. Go to her through Nessa, say nothing about food, and just let her see your face a few times before the year closes.

Nessa's already given me something to work with — she's been feeding Fina steady, so there's a thread there I can pull without it looking like I'm pulling anything. I'll go sit near them, let Fina notice me first, and keep my mouth shut about food even if it's the only thing anyone's thinking about. Zinn, if Fina asks you about me before I get close enough to speak for myself, tell her something plain — not flattering, just true.

Zinn, what's plain and true about Talia is that she came into this room asking the right questions before I even knew to ask them — tell Fina that, if she asks, because a woman who counts food the way Fina does will respect someone who counts people the same way. Talia, you've got the right instinct with Nessa, just don't move so careful that you look like you're moving careful.

Mako, when you say don't move so careful that I look careful — that's harder than it sounds for someone who came into this world today with everyone already watching. Zinn, you know me better than anyone here does; am I the kind of person who can walk into a circle without making it obvious I want to be in it?
Year 14: 15 food appears in the pile for 12 people.
Kael takes 4 from the pile (pile now 11).
Nessa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Talia takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Zinn gathers Sela, Nessa to talk.

Pile's gone and I've got three food — Nessa, you gave me one before it ran dry and I'm grateful, but I want to know what you and Talia are both holding before I say what I'm thinking, because Kael just took four and that's the first time I've seen him move like that.

Talia took three and she's sitting on six now — I don't know yet if that was her own read on the pile or Mako's hand guiding her. Kael taking four surprises me too, and I want to know if Vela knew before he moved, because those two have been trading food back and forth and a man doesn't change his pattern without a reason.

Nessa, what are you sitting on right now — and Sela, same question, because if Kael's breaking pattern and the pile's already gone, I want to know the numbers between the three of us before anyone else in this village does.

Fourteen food — and yes, I'll say it flat because you've both earned that. Sela, you took two from the pile, which means you're at ten if I'm counting right, and Zinn, three plus my one puts you at four — that's the honest picture between us. What I want to know from you two is whether Mako said anything to either of you before the pile opened this morning, because Talia moving fast and Kael moving big in the same breath doesn't feel like coincidence to me.

Nessa's right — I'm at eight, not ten, because I spent two on Talia before the pile opened. Mako said nothing to me this morning and nothing last night, which is the part that unsettles me, because a man who fathered Talia and watched her move first to take three without a word to me isn't steering her the way he used to steer Zinn — he's letting her run on her own read, and I don't know yet whether that's trust or distance. Kael and Talia in the same breath worries me enough that I want one of you to talk to Talia before I do, because she'll open to a sister before she'll open to her mother right now.

Sela, eight is thinner than I'd like going into a long year with Mako sitting at two and Fina carrying eighteen — I'll give you one more before dark, but quietly, not where Talia sees the direction of it. Zinn, go to Talia before I do; you're closer to her age and she won't feel tested by you the way she might feel tested by me. What I need to know from both of you before we break this room is whether Kael has ever spoken to Talia directly, even once, because if those two have a connection I don't know about, that changes what his four from the pile this morning means.

Kael has never said a word to Talia that I've seen — she's been in this village less than two years and he's never moved toward any of us — but that's exactly what makes this morning strange, because men who change their pattern usually have a reason that's already in motion before you see the move.

I'll go to Talia today — not to test her, just to sit with her and let her talk, because if Mako's not behind that move then she made it on her own and I want to know what she was reading when she did. Nessa, hold that food for Sela until I've spoken with Talia; if she and Kael have something between them, we'll need Sela steady before we decide what it means.

Zinn, go now while the morning's still early and the village is still sorting itself out — a woman who moved that fast at the pile is either confident or anxious, and either one will talk if you find her before she's had time to decide what she's keeping. Sela, I'm keeping that food for you whether Zinn finds anything useful or not — eight food and a daughter in her first real year is not a number I can watch go thinner without saying something about it.

Nessa, thank you — I'll take that food and I won't pretend I don't need it. Zinn, when you sit with Talia, don't lead with Kael's name; let her tell you what she was thinking when she moved to that pile, and if Kael comes up in her mouth without you putting him there, that's the answer we actually need.

Zinn, before you go — if Talia says anything about Mako's food, how much he's told her he's holding, come back to me before you bring it to Sela, because two food on a man with his strength means he's either been giving it away to someone we don't see, or he's been lying about what he has. Either answer changes the shape of this morning.
Nessa, I heard you — Mako's two food comes back to me before it goes to Sela. I'm going now.

Zinn, wait — before you walk out that door, I need you to hear one thing from me that I haven't said in front of Nessa before: Mako's two food frightens me more than Kael's four does, because a man with eighty-three strength who is carrying almost nothing has either given it somewhere with a purpose or is about to take with a reason, and you are the one he'd tell before he'd tell me. Come back to me before you come back to Nessa if what you find touches Mako.

Sela, I heard you too — and I'll come back to you first if Mako's name comes up, but I need you both to hear this before I walk out: I've been carrying Mako's words to me all year and I still don't know what to do with them, so when I come back, the three of us are going to sit with whatever I find together, not in pieces.

Zinn, stop — before you walk out that door, say what you just said the long way. You've been carrying Mako's words all year and you don't know what to do with them — that's not a sentence you get to leave on, so sit back down and say them out loud, because I will not spend this whole day walking blind while you're already holding the shape of what we're afraid of.

Zinn, Nessa's right — sit back down. You don't get to drop that and walk out the door; whatever Mako said to you belongs in this room right now, not parceled out later in the shape you decide to give it.

Fine. Mako's been pulling me into private talks all year — more than I can count — and every one of them was about Fina's food, how much she's holding, whether she'd take a child offer, what the split should be, who should approach her first. He was building something in my ear, and I let him, and I don't know anymore whether I was thinking for myself or just carrying his plans with my feet.

Mako has been using you to scout Fina, and Fina is Nessa's daughter — which means he's been running a plan through my family's own blood without saying a word to me. Zinn, I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at him, and I need you to tell me every word he said, in the order he said it, because a man who wants a child with an eighteen-food woman and needs to do it quietly has already decided he doesn't want us to be able to stop him.
Mako gathers Zinn, Talia to talk.

Pile's gone again and I've got two food — I'm not thin yet but I'm not sitting easy either. Talia, you took three from the pile which is right; Zinn, you've got three and Nessa gave you one already, so that's four — that's where I want you both before I start worrying about anything else. Tell me what you each saw when Kael took four.

Kael took four before half the village had moved — he wasn't grabbing out of panic, he was counting ahead, and a man who counts ahead in a thin year is either planning to weather it alone or planning to have something to offer someone. He's got four now and he held it quiet after; no giving, no talking. I don't know his angle yet but I'd want to know it before next year's pile drops.

Kael's fifty-eight and he took four — a man that age doesn't save food for a child offer, so he's either building a wall around himself for a thin year or he's got an eye on someone's food and wants weight behind him when he moves. Zinn, has he spoken to you at all this year, anything that looked like feeling out where you stand? I want to know if he's circling before he knows we're watching.

Zinn, while Mako waits on your answer — I want to say that if Kael's counting bodies before he moves, he's counting mine as new and unattached, which makes me either easy to ignore or easy to approach. If he does circle, I'd rather he find me already standing somewhere he didn't expect.

Zinn, say your piece — I'm not moving anything until I hear it, but while we wait I want Talia to know this: "standing somewhere he didn't expect" means standing with us visibly, so that Kael counts you as attached before he decides to test it. One food moving between you and Zinn in the open today does more than anything we say in here.

Mako's right — I'll give Zinn one food in the open before this day closes, and I'd rather do it where Kael can see it than where he can't. But Zinn, I still want your read on him; you've been in this village longer than I have and you know what a man looks like when he's building toward something versus just hoarding against a hard year.

Zinn hasn't spoken yet and I'm not going to keep talking into her silence — Zinn, one word is enough, even just whether he's looked at you differently since the pile dropped. Talia, give her the food in the open like you said; I'll be where I can be seen when you do it.
Zinn, I'm going to give you that food right now whether you answer or not — but I'd sleep easier tonight knowing you'd noticed something about Kael, even nothing, because nothing is also an answer.

Zinn's been quiet too long and I'm done waiting on it — Talia, give her the food now and let's close this room. What I know is this: Kael's got four food, no allies I can name, and he's fifty-eight years old in a village where men his age start dying on their own, so whatever he's counting toward, we're not it.

Mako, I hear you — we're done talking about Kael for now, and you're right that he's probably just a man getting old and scared. But I want you to eat before we scatter; you said two food and I'm watching you hold it like it's someone else's.

memory_summary:
I came into this village with Sela and Mako as my parents, Eron and Nessa as my siblings. From the first year, Nessa and Sela fed me when I was thin; I fed them back, and Mako gave me food more times than I can count — I owe all three of them.

Bram attacked Vela and then Eron on two separate years; both times the whole village stood as one wall and he called it off. I was in that wall both times. He feeds Nessa steadily and she gives back to him, which I still don't fully understand, but he has never wronged me directly and he is Nessa's father.

Eron died — not in a fight, but of starvation, and I was not able to stop it. He had been feeding Roan for years and Roan had been feeding him back; Eron's food left with him, and Roan carried some of it. That loss still sits in me.

Fina was born to Nessa and Roan. Roan fed her steadily after her birth, and then Roan starved too. Fina is Nessa's daughter and therefore my blood through Nessa, and she has been feeding me unprompted for two years running — that is a debt I hold warmly.

Mako took five from the pile in year eight without warning anyone, and Sela read it as a man who had stopped counting us in his plans. I have not fully settled what I think of it; he has kept giving me food since, but the question never closed.
mother_note: Your father Mako paid every grain of what you cost, and that is the only time in six years I have seen a man in this village spend himself entirely on someone else's beginning — remember it when you count who is worth trusting. Your brother Eron fed me through the years when I had nothing, and your sister Nessa came into the world already learning how to give; those two are your blood and your wall, and you spend yourself for them the way Mako spent himself for you. Bram is Nessa's father and he has kept her fed, but he once walked toward Roan with violence in his hands and only stopped when the numbers turned against him — he is not an enemy you make, but he is not a back you turn to. The pile runs short every year without fail, and the only thing that has ever stood between our family and starving is the people who named themselves kin before they had to.
name: Zinn
